source.title: Dynamic Reflections: Probing Video Representations with Text Alignment
source.authors: Tyler Zhu; Teng-Da Han; Leonidas J. Guibas; Viorica Patraucean; M. Ovsjanikov

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendix are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study discusses training-time scaling laws by analogy, but does not measure held-out language-model pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or training compute. Its own scaling results concern video-text alignment as test-time frames and captions vary.
record.gate_note: The paper reports fitted scaling curves for video-text alignment, not the cross-entropy loss or compute-optimal allocation named in the claim. Those alignment results are recorded as related findings with versions ["none"]. Its downstream correlations relate alignment to task performance, not performance to scale or pretraining loss. No results from the cited scaling-law studies are counted.
record.test_reason: The paper fits a test-time saturation power law to video-text mutual k-NN alignment as frames and captions given at inference vary. It does not measure pretraining loss against parameters, tokens or compute, nor fit-dependence of training-time laws. It cites Kaplan and Hoffmann only by analogy. Its downstream correlations tie alignment, not scale or pretraining loss, to task performance. No version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct in substance. The authors also stress that alignment can roughly double without retraining. They say native video models use temporal information better than image encoders. They propose alignment as a zero-shot proxy for video representation quality.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses mutual k-NN alignment and fits a saturation curve over test-time frames and captions; it does not use a language-model pretraining-loss scaling-law recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Alignment varies with the number of video frames and captions, vision model, dataset, and encoder pair; fitted parameters also differ across models and datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: Video-text mutual k-NN alignment against Gemma 2-9b-it rises with test-time frames and captions. A saturation power law fits it with R2 0.944–0.998 across 11 vision models on VaTeX and PVD. Video models show smaller frame exponents α than image models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Test-time cross-modal alignment follows a saturating power law in the number of input frames and captions.

record.problems: The reported fits concern alignment rather than pretraining loss. The scaling-law evidence is primarily presented as fitted parameters and R2 values; uncertainty intervals for those fit parameters are not stated. PVD uses synthesized captions, and the paper notes that Perception Encoder was trained on that dataset.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible results omitted. Downstream alignment/performance correlations are not included as rows because they measure association with alignment, not downstream predictability from model scale or pretraining loss.

untested.parts: Pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute
Extrapolation from small to large training runs
Architecture shape effects on loss at fixed parameters
Training-time power-law loss in other modalities or regimes; only test-time alignment is fitted
Downstream performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss
Setup or fitting-choice dependence of training-time laws

record.verdict_notes: The analogy to Chinchilla's L(N,D)=E+A/N^a+B/D^b is conceptual only (App. B). The 1-to-10 caption gain (~60%, y=1.6x−0.018) is also test-time and unrelated to the versions.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or training compute.
Whether laws fitted on small language-model pretraining runs predict the losses of substantially larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations for language-model pretraining.
Effect of architecture details on language-model pretraining loss at fixed parameter count.
The target is pretraining loss under other modalities or training regimes; this paper instead measures test-time video-text alignment.
Downstream performance as a function of model scale or pretraining loss; the paper correlates downstream results with alignment scores instead.
Whether language-model pretraining loss curves or compute-optimal splits depend on fitting choices or depart from power laws.
